items.text: Autistic burnout can take skills you've had for years — speech, cooking, driving, replying to a text. That's not regression. That's depletion. Skills on loan, not skills gone.
items.rationale: Names the specific, rarely-validated experience of skill loss during burnout. 'Skills on loan' reframes it as temporary depletion rather than permanent deterioration — the kind of precision that generates deep recognition.

items.text: If you've lost abilities during autistic burnout and quietly wondered if you're broken — you're not. The skills didn't leave. The system ran out of power to run them.
items.rationale: Shifts the internal narrative from 'I am deteriorating' to 'I am depleted'. A second angle on the same phenomenon that lands differently — more personal, more direct address.

items.text: It's not the task. It's the demand shape wrapped around it. A PDAer can desperately want that concert — the fixed time slot is still unbearable. 'Just do what you enjoy' misses this entirely.
items.rationale: Delivers the demand-sensitivity insight via a single vivid example. Quotable and portable. Gives non-PDA readers a genuinely new mental model without requiring prior vocabulary.

items.text: If your nervous system is running an autonomy-protection programme, is 'pathological' even the right word? The PDA community is actively rethinking the name — and the argument isn't just semantic.
items.rationale: Opens a live, unresolved community debate without taking a side. Language debates draw genuine engagement in neurodivergent spaces because naming shapes self-understanding and clinical treatment.

items.text: Remote work wasn't a perk for autistic workers. It was an accommodation that existed briefly by accident. Now it's being taken away — and UK employment tribunals are documenting the harm.
items.rationale: 'Accommodation by accident' is precise and non-hyperbolic. Grounds the systemic critique in documented legal evidence rather than anecdote. Wide reach beyond already-diagnosed readers.

items.text: 45% of neurodivergent employees are exhausted at work always or often. 30% of neurotypical peers say the same. That gap isn't attitude. It's what masking all day costs.
items.rationale: Hard data makes the masking cost concrete and shareable. The closing line reframes the number as mechanistic, not moral — removing the 'trying hard enough' accusation.
items.sensitivity_flag: Verify the CIPD figures (45% / 30%) directly in the HR Magazine source before publishing — cited via briefing summary, not primary CIPD document.

items.text: A late autism or ADHD diagnosis doesn't give you an answer. It gives you a hundred new questions about your own history. The relief is real. So is the grief. Both make sense.
items.rationale: Names the relief-and-grief duality that public discourse almost never articulates clearly. Self-contained, deeply recognisable to late-diagnosed adults, and invites rather than closes conversation.

items.text: Getting diagnosed at 35 isn't like learning new information. It forces a reread of every job you lost, every relationship that frayed. Researchers call it developmental reorganisation. That tracks.
items.rationale: Validates the destabilising nature of late diagnosis without calling the diagnosis itself bad. 'That tracks' grounds the scientific framing without overstating it.
items.sensitivity_flag: Source is practitioner Substack, not a peer-reviewed journal. 'Developmental reorganisation' is their framing. Consider softening to 'some researchers describe it as' if posting to an audience likely to scrutinise citations.

items.text: Rest is necessary for autistic burnout recovery — not sufficient. If you're still masking at home, the load doesn't actually drop. Recovery needs reduced masking, not just reduced activity.
items.rationale: Gives people who've tried resting and found it didn't work a specific, named explanation. Removes self-blame and points toward something actionable without prescribing a protocol.
items.sensitivity_flag: This is practitioner consensus, not RCT-level evidence. The post is appropriately hedged ('necessary but not sufficient') but avoid language that implies this is a complete or guaranteed recovery framework.

items.text: 'Put your shoes on' can register as a threat in a PDA nervous system. That's not defiance. That's a body running a survival programme. Naughty is the wrong frame entirely.
items.rationale: Shifts a parent's entire reading of PDA behaviour in two sentences. The survival-programme frame is the community's preferred explanatory layer and maps cleanly to what the research supports.

items.text: The sick-day paradox: the day you're officially allowed to do nothing is often the day you can finally do something. That's not laziness. That's what happens when demand pressure drops.
items.rationale: Shareable, punchy, and directly rebuts 'you can do it when you want to'. Maps to demand-sensitivity without requiring readers to already know the terminology.

items.text: If you were diagnosed autistic or ADHD as an adult: was it more relief, more grief, or something the word 'diagnosis' doesn't quite capture? Asking because that complexity rarely gets named.
items.rationale: Invites genuine conversation rather than passive engagement. 'Something the word doesn't quite capture' signals that complicated, ambivalent, or contradictory answers are equally welcome.
